findings.finding: 0% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 7 of 48 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Wrenford "dineli" = food: misheard: tineli → dineli (generation 21) · Wrenford "thela" = no: misheard: thele → thela (generation 12) · Oakhollow "dineli" = food: misheard: tineli → dineli (generation 21)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.58, p = 0.049, n = 12. Most used: two (2% replaced per generation), tools (25% replaced per generation), no (8% replaced per generation); least: five (34%), four (45%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: 2 founding families still alive. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.50, p = 0.016, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
